figures.caption: Fig. 1. Dynamics-feature alignment for perturbation recovery. An external force at t2 perturbs the humanoid and drives the generated dynamics features away from the reference distribution. ADP encourages recovery by regularizing the perturbed windows toward this distribution, resulting in stable locomotion at t3.

Fig. 4. Qualitative hardware demonstration of ADP on the real robot under repeated external pushes. The overlaid snapshots show the robot transitioning from nominal walking to a perturbed state and recovering under subsequent perturbations.

Fig. 5. Normalized reference deviation in dynamics-feature and kinematicfeature representations under a lateral ∆vy = 3.0 m/s push. Lines and bands denote medians and IQRs over 106 pooled non-fallen rollout episodes.

Fig. 6. Effect of temporal dynamics-feature window length K on normalized recovery metrics. Larger K provides temporal context for contact switching, force modulation, and momentum recovery, but overly long windows can degrade training stability. Lower-is-better metrics are inverted after normalization, so higher scores indicate better performance.

Fig. 2. Overview of the proposed Adversarial Dynamics Priors (ADP) framework. (a) SRBD-based trajectory optimization generates reference locomotion trajectories, from which dynamics features are extracted to construct Ddyn. (b) During policy training, policy-generated windows are evaluated by a discriminator trained with Ddyn, producing the dynamics prior reward rD t . The policy is trained with the task reward rG t , dynamics prior reward rD t , and regularization reward rR t .

Fig. 3. Time-series perturbation recovery under a lateral push. Red, orange, blue, and green curves denote Vanilla RL, Dynamics Reward, AMP, and ADP, respectively. Lines show the mean and translucent bands show the Interquartile Range (IQR) over 32 environments; the panels show velocity tracking error, base attitude error, and base roll/pitch angular velocity.
